name: The Gros Tilleul de Samoëns

location.address: Place du Gros Tilleul, 74340 Samoëns, Haute-Savoie, France

access: Free, in the open village square at all times
transport: No train station in Samoens; regular bus from Cluses SNCF station (approx 30-40 min), or by car
verify_notes: Tradition (repeated by French Wikipedia's Arbre remarquable infobox and the village's own tourism site) holds it was planted in 1438, giving roughly 586 years as of 2024/roughly 590 today; kept broad since the planting date rests on local tradition rather than a ring count. Two sources agree: girth about 9m, height about 20m, species Tilleul a grandes feuilles (Tilia platyphyllos). Both agree the tree grows on the square that bears its name (Place du Gros Tilleul) in the middle of the village. Story: named alongside Samoens' other landmark (Le Criou mountain) as one of the village's two emblems; from the 16th century, before Samoens had a town hall, the council of syndics (the village's governing body, whose 1431 founding right from Duke Amedee VIII of Savoy the tree is said to commemorate) held its assemblies under its branches, and it remains where important village meetings and gatherings take place today. Listed among France's officially registered 'arbres remarquables' (association A.R.B.R.E.S.) and appears on the Haute-Savoie DREAL list of sites classes et inscrits (Liste des sites classes et inscrits de la Haute-Savoie), i.e. a legally protected/classified site. Also promoted by the Haute-Savoie tourism Wikipedia article alongside Samoens' Jardin botanique alpin La Jaysinia as one of the village's two named sights. No dated recent photo found (Commons image is from 2013), but the village's own tourism page describing it as still standing centre-square was last updated 2023-05-10, and a legally classified, actively-promoted village landmark going unremarked-on if it had died is very unlikely; flagged only for the lack of a post-2020 dated photo. Alone at 46.6km from the nearest published tree, so it would need to be its own place; passes the single-tree-destination test on the strength of being one of only two named landmarks of the village (with the botanical garden), officially classified, and centuries-documented, though it is more a village-square icon locals gather at than a pilgrimage destination in its own right, worth noting for the writer.

name: The Tilleul de Pérouges (Liberty Tree)

location.address: Place de la Halle (Place du Tilleul), Cite medievale de Perouges, 01800 Perouges, Ain, France
location.neighbourhood: Central square of the walled medieval town

access: Free, open square (Acces: Libre per the official DREAL fact sheet); parking at the tree itself has been banned since 2010 to protect the roots
transport: Gare de Meximieux-Perouges (SNCF/TER), then about 1.5km / 20-25 minutes on foot uphill into the walled town
verify_notes: Planted 21 April 1792 as a Liberty Tree (arbre de la liberte) celebrating the French Revolution, in the exact centre of the Place de la Halle of the Cite medievale de Perouges, a walled hilltop medieval town in the Ain and one of France's officially listed 'Plus Beaux Villages'; the square is even called Place du Tilleul after it. Confirmed by two independent sources: the official DREAL (French environment ministry) 'site classe' fact sheet for the tree, and French Wikipedia's dedicated article (citing the classification records). DREAL sheet states it is the ONLY classified tree ('arbre remarquable') in the entire Ain department (classified as a site naturel under the May 1930 sites law), which is strong evidence of genuine fame rather than routine listing. Height fell from 20m in 1948 to about 8m today after heavy limbs broke under their own weight and had to be cut back; trunk is hollow and the crown (described as looking like butterfly wings) is now held up by seven wooden props. species is only given as 'tilleul' (lime) in both sources, exact species (platyphyllos/cordata/europaea) not specified by either, so left as Tilia sp. and flagged. SOURCE DISAGREEMENT on trajectory: French Wikipedia (undated prose) says the tree 'se meurt peu a peu' (is dying little by little); the official DREAL sheet says it reached senescence and has since STABILISED, crediting a ban on winter road salt at its roots (which was poisoning it) for the improvement; noted here rather than picking a winner. DREAL sheet appears to date from around 2009 (states the tree was '217 ans', i.e. 217 years after the 1792 planting = 2009) so is not brand new, but Wikimedia Commons holds dated photographs from October 2021 and 2022 (Category:Tilleul de Perouges: 'Le tilleul de Perouges et ses renforts en avril 2021.jpg', 'Perouges, place de la Halle dite du Tilleul, 2022.jpg') showing the propped, leafy tree still standing in the square, which is the best available 'alive recently' evidence; no report of its death or removal found anywhere. Passes the single-tree-destination test comfortably: it is the ONLY classified tree in its whole department, the visual and symbolic centrepiece of a famous, actively-touristed medieval walled town (people already travel to Perouges for the town itself, and the tree is the literal centre of the main square they stand in), and it carries its own real story (French Revolution liberty tree, most such trees did not survive the Restoration, this one did).

name: The Chene de Cantaure
age_estimate: roughly 700-800 years (at least since the 14th century)

location.address: Quartier de Cantaure, about 3km south of the village of Lue, 40210 Lue, Landes, France

access: Free; stands on communal land right beside a rural lane, open at all times, no ticket or gate
transport: Rural; no train or bus service nearby, reached by car only, about 3km south of Lue village centre
verify_notes: A pedunculate oak dating from at least the 14th century (French Wikipedia's sourced article, citing the commune's own interpretive panel and a published 'Dictionnaire historique des Landes'), awarded the official national label 'Arbre remarquable de France' by the association A.R.B.R.E.S. on 3 May 2011. Girth given as 8m at normal measuring height and 11m at ground level (the wider figure is a base/root-flare measurement, not the trunk, so girth_cm records the 8m figure); height 18-20m; trunk hollow, splitting into two large master branches forming a big fork. The land and tree were donated to the commune of Lue by the owner, Michel Harribey, on 26 March 1997, and the commune has looked after it since. Sourced independently in a Sud Ouest newspaper piece (confirmed to exist and to cover this tree via its own metadata/headline, though the body text is paywalled) about the tree being used in June 2019 as the filming location for the final scene of the short film 'Liska: l'appel de l'innocence', published 6 Aug 2021. Best story for the writer: the Haute-Lande ethnologist Felix Arnaudin photographed the oak in 1899 (photo held at the Musee d'Aquitaine) and wrote that around 1870 he personally stopped tenant farmers from cutting it down for firewood by rushing to alert the landowner, saving it at the last minute; a local legend also has Pope Leon IX passing by and Pope Clement V stopping near it around 1310, though that is recorded as legend rather than fact. Photographs on Wikimedia Commons include one uploaded August 2023 and the site was reportedly visited/consulted by the Wikipedia editor in July 2023, both recent 'still standing' evidence; no death or felling reported anywhere. Passes the single-tree-destination test: nationally labelled remarkable tree, a documented near-miss with the axe made famous by a well-known regional ethnologist, and a real story (not just 'old tree in a forest').

name: The Chataignier de l'Eraudiere
age_estimate: 800 to 1200 years (local tradition holds it was planted in 756 AD)

location.address: Square de la Mee, rue du Chateau de l'Eraudiere, 44300 Nantes, Loire-Atlantique, France

access: Free, in an open public square (Square de la Mee); the tree itself sits inside a low protective fence to stop trampling of its roots, but is fully visible and the square is open at all times
transport: Busway/tram line C6, Eraudiere stop, right by the square
verify_notes: Nantes Metropole's own official tourism page (current, last updated December 2025) names this as one of the city's remarkable trees: 'aurait entre 800 et 1200 ans selon les sources' (would be between 800 and 1200 years old according to sources), 15m tall, 12m wide, with two huge tentacle-like branches that make it look like 'a living sculpture'. A specialist tree blog (krapooarboricole, 2011, citing Nantes' own parks and green-spaces department) gives the fuller story: popular tradition holds it was planted in the year 756 (which would make it around 1270 years old and a genuine millennial tree), but the city's own green-spaces service more conservatively puts it at around 800 years; kept as the vague range the sources actually give rather than picked apart. Considered the oldest tree ('doyen') of the whole Loire-Atlantique department. Trunk girth measured at over 10m by the city (informally re-measured at 11.70m at 1m height by a local guide, which the source itself flags as an unscientific method, so girth_cm is set to the more often-repeated 10m/1000cm figure); trunk is thick, spiralled and hollowing with age. It once stood in the private grounds of the chateau de l'Eraudiere, of the same name, that has since been swallowed by the city's growth; today it stands in its own dedicated public square, fenced only to protect the roots from foot traffic, and still produces chestnuts every year. The Nantes Metropole source being a live official city page updated within the last year is itself strong 'alive now' evidence, on top of the specific 2011 account of a recent guided visit. Location is precise: the OSM coordinate for Square de la Mee (47.2449639, -1.5418239) matches the candidate coordinate almost exactly, and the square exists specifically around this one tree. Passes the single-tree-destination test easily: official oldest tree of its department, actively promoted by the city itself as a sight to see, with a genuine legend (a millennium-plus planting date) attached.

name: The Platane de Prety

location.address: Place de l'eglise, near the Eglise Notre-Dame, 71290 Prety, Saone-et-Loire, France

access: Free, standing in the open at a village crossroads next to the church, always accessible
transport: No station in Prety; Tournus SNCF station (Paris-Lyon main line) is about 3km away by road
verify_notes: A monumental plane tree planted in 1801 on a mound at a crossroads by the village church, replacing an 'orme de justice' (justice elm), reportedly to celebrate the Concordat that let priests return to France after the Revolution. Two independent sources agree closely: French Wikipedia's Prety article (citing an official DREAL/Ministry of Ecological Transition site-classe fact sheet) gives height 34m, trunk perimeter 5.7m, canopy spread 36m; the regional heritage federation FAPPAH's own page on Prety independently gives height 33.5m and repeats the 1801/Concordat story and the justice-elm detail. Formally protected: classified as a 'site classe' (natural monument) on 25 August 1909 (confirmed via French Wikipedia's 'Liste des sites classes et inscrits de Saone-et-Loire', citing the same government fact sheet with the exact date), which is an unusually early classification, decades before most of France's remarkable-tree protections. Reportedly one of the few plane trees never pruned since planting, left to develop its natural, well-balanced crown at the crossroads. The government fact-sheet host (piece-jointe-carto.developpement-durable.gouv.fr) hung on a direct fetch (curl timed out after 20s) so its content is only known via the two Wikipedia citations quoting it; noting this for the blocklist. No post-2020 dated photograph found (Commons images are from 2015), and a 2020 tree-enthusiast blog post title ('De 1801 a nos jours il regne ici en toute quietude') implies it was still standing then but the page itself would not load to confirm the body text, so flagged for lack of very recent 'still standing' confirmation; no report of death, felling or storm damage found anywhere, and a tree under formal state protection since 1909 going unremarked if lost seems unlikely. Passes the single-tree-destination test: one of the earliest legally protected trees in France, with a real historical story (a Revolution-era political tree marking the restoration of the clergy) and an exceptional, never-pruned form.

name: The Arburacellu (the Bird Tree)

location.address: Strada di u Listincu, near Gattone, 20240 Ghisonaccia, Haute-Corse, Corsica, France

access: Free, beside a rural lane; actively promoted by the local tourist office as one of the area's 'not to be missed' sights, implying open public access, though exact approach/parking not confirmed
transport: Rural Corsican plain, reached by car; nearest town is Ghisonaccia
verify_notes: A cork oak (chene-liege) estimated at 200-250 years old, height about 15m, trunk circumference about 4m. Its fame has nothing to do with age and everything to do with shape: probably following a lightning strike (which disrupted normal sap flow) the cork bark grew into three dramatic outgrowths that together look, from the right angle, exactly like a giant bird of prey with raised head and spread wings; the burnt/hollow core is visible evidence of past fire damage. Discovered only in 2017 by a local resident (M. Goletto) and his granddaughter while out foraging for wild asparagus; he brought it to the same person who had earlier gotten Ghisonaccia's other remarkable tree (a c. 1000 year old pistachier lentisque) officially recognised, and it was entered in France's 2018 'Arbre de l'Annee' (Tree of the Year) contest, organised by Terre Sauvage magazine and the ONF (Office National des Forets). It WON the public prize with 3053 of over 12000 votes cast (confirmed directly on the contest organiser's own site, arbredelannee.com, not just via a secondary citation), and went on to place 4th in the European Tree of the Year 2019 contest with 29,140 of 311,772 votes (per French Wikipedia, citing treeoftheyear.org). Confirmed independently by Ghisonaccia's own town hall (mairie) website and by the Corse Orientale intercommunal tourist office, which lists it among its official 'must-see' sights (Les Incontournables) alongside a description of the discovery story. Location is about as confirmed as this project's bar allows: OpenStreetMap carries an individually tagged natural=tree node at this exact coordinate, named 'l'Arbre Oiseau', on Strada di u Listincu near the Gattone hamlet. No indication anywhere of the tree being dead, removed or storm-felled since its 2018 win; being a national contest winner actively promoted by both the commune and the regional tourist board is strong evidence it is being maintained and shown off, not neglected. Passes the single-tree-destination test better than any other candidate checked this pass: this is a tree people found out about BECAUSE of a national popularity contest and now visit specifically to see its bird shape, the purest form of 'would someone travel for this one tree'.
